children.title: 5.2. Joint Probability Mass Functions
children.markdown: Many real-world scenarios involve multiple random quantities that interact with each other. To analyze such situations, we need to understand how random variables behave together. Joint probability mass functions provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing multiple discrete random variables simultaneously.

children.title: Road Map 🧭
children.markdown:
- Define joint probability mass functions for multiple discrete random variables.

- Explore tabular and functional representations of joint PMFs.

- Understand how to derive marginal distributions from joint distributions.

- Identify when random variables are independent based on their joint PMF.

children.title: 5.2.1. Joint Probability Mass Functions
children.markdown: When dealing with a single discrete random variable, we used a probability mass function (PMF) to specify the probabilities associated with each possible value. We now extend this concept to multiple random variables.

children.title: Definition
children.markdown:
The joint probability mass function (joint PMF) for two discrete random variables and is denoted by , and it gives the probability that equals some value and equals some value simultaneously: 𝑋 𝑌 𝑝𝑋,𝑌 𝑋 𝑥 𝑌 𝑦

$$p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = P ( \{ X = x \} \cap \{ Y = y \} ) .$$

Concisely, we also write 𝑝𝑋,𝑌 (𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝑃(𝑋 = 𝑥, 𝑌 = 𝑦).

This definition extends naturally to more than two random variables. For example, the joint PMF for three random variables , , and would be denoted as . 𝑋 𝑌 𝑍 𝑝𝑋,𝑌 ,𝑍(𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧)

children.title: Support
children.markdown:
The support of a joint PMF is the set of all pairs for which the PMF assigns a positive probability: (𝑥, 𝑦)

$$\sup p ( X , Y ) = \{ ( x , y ) \ | \ p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) > 0 \} .$$

children.title: Representations of Joint PMFs
children.markdown: Joint probability mass functions can be represented in several ways.

children.title: Tabular Form
children.markdown: For two discrete random variables with finite supports, we can represent the joint PMF as a table. Each cell contains the probability that equals the row value and equals the column value. 𝑋 𝑌

children.title: Validity of a Joint PMF
children.markdown: Like single-variable PMFs, joint PMFs must satisfy the following two axioms.

children.title: 1. Non-negativity
children.markdown: For all values of and , 𝑥 𝑦 0 ≤ 𝑝𝑋,𝑌 (𝑥, 𝑦) ≤ 1.

children.title: 2. Total probability of 1
children.markdown:
The sum of all probabilities in the joint PMF must equal 1:

$$\sum _ { ( x , y ) \in \text {supp} ( X , Y ) } p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = 1 .$$

children.title: Marginal PMF
children.markdown: A marginal PMF is the individual probability mass function of a random variable that forms a joint PMF with others.

children.title: Deriving Marginal PMFs from a Joint PMF
children.markdown:
One of the most important operations we can perform with a joint PMF is deriving marginal PMFs for individual random variables.

To find the marginal PMF , we sum the joint PMF for each fixed value over all possible values of : 𝑝𝑋(𝑥) 𝑥 𝑌

$$p _ { X } ( x ) = \sum _ { y \colon p _ { Y } ( y ) > 0 } p _ { X , Y } ( x , y )$$

Similarly, to find the marginal PMF , we sum the joint PMF for each fixed value over all possible values of : 𝑝𝑌 (𝑦) 𝑦 𝑋

$$p _ { Y } ( y ) = \sum _ { x \colon p _ { X } ( x ) > 0 } p _ { X , Y } ( x , y )$$

In tabular form, the marginal PMF values are computed as row-wise or column-wise sums of the joint PMF and are often recorded in the margins of the table-hence the name marginal PMF.

children.title: Marginal PMFs and the Law of Partitions
children.markdown:

children.title: Definition
children.markdown:
Two discrete random variables and are independent if and only if their joint PMF factors as the product of their marginal PMFs for all values in the support. Mathematically, they are independent if and only if 𝑋 𝑌

$$p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = p _ { X } ( x ) p _ { Y } ( y ) \text { for all } ( x , y ) \in \sup p ( X , Y ) .$$

children.title: What Does It Mean?
children.markdown:
Independence of random variables and means that knowing the value of one provides no information about the value of the other. 𝑋 𝑌

With respect to the previously learned concept of independence of two events, this means that any event written in terms of is independent of any event expressed in terms of . 𝑋 𝑌

In our dice example, and are independent because 𝑋 𝑌

$$p _ { X , Y } ( x , y ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 4 } = \frac { 1 } { 4 } \times \frac { 1 } { 6 } = p _ { X } ( x ) p _ { Y } ( y )$$

for all values of and in the support. 𝑥 𝑦

children.title: Be cautious 🛑
children.markdown: Independence is an important property that often simplifies probability calculations. However, its convenient properties should only be used when the independence of and is provided or shown mathematically. 𝑋 𝑌

Since the requirement for independence is for all possible pairs, and has already failed the criterion. Therefore, they are dependent. 𝑝𝑋,𝑌 (𝑥, 𝑦) = 𝑝𝑋(𝑥)𝑝𝑌 (𝑦) 𝑋 𝑌

A joint distribution can encode constraints (a bounded sum in the previous example) that never appear in the marginals alone. Whenever the joint PMF doesn't factor, dependence is at play.

children.title: Key Takeaways 📝
children.markdown:
1. A joint probability mass function specifies the probability of two or more discrete random variables taking on specific values simultaneously.

2. Joint PMFs must satisfy the basic probability axioms: non-negativity and summing to 1 over the entire support.

3. Marginal distributions can be derived from a joint PMF by summing over all possible values of the other variable(s).

4. Random variables are independent if and only if their joint PMF equals the product of their marginal PMFs for all values in the support.

5. When random variables are dependent, their joint distribution contains important information about how they relate to each other that isn't captured by their marginal distributions alone.
